A halo in a clustered Universe

How gravitational clustering, uncertain distances and coherent environments shape the galaxies we assign to a halo.

Physical foundations of a conditional marked Cox model.

Dan Benayoun · Updated 5 October 2026 · 36 min read

A concentration of galaxies on the sky is an invitation to ask a three-dimensional question. Which galaxies belong to the same halo? Which occupy its correlated surroundings? Which only appear nearby because the sky has compressed their distances into two coordinates?

The difficulty is not simply that redshifts are uncertain. Galaxies outside the halo form groups and filaments of their own. They can provide a coherent alternative explanation for a concentration that a uniform background would assign to the halo.

This article builds a conditional model of that competition. We begin with a projected member population, derive why a halo's average environment differs from a random location, and describe how particular environments fluctuate around that average. We then connect true redshift to the information recorded for each galaxy and derive a likelihood that retains both the locations and the number of observations.

The construction has several kinds of foundations. Gravitational dynamics motivates correlations. Probability identities determine how conditioning, observation and superposition work. Calibrated tracer relations and explicitly chosen closures join the pieces. Keeping those roles visible is part of understanding what a membership probability means.

1. One sightline, several physical populations

Let the distinguished halo have angular centre ϑ∗ and redshift z∗. Within a fixed observed region D, the catalogue records angular positions, disjoint observed population classes a, and photometric data d:

(1)X={(ϑi,ai,di):i=1,…,n}.

The classes might distinguish selected galaxy populations with different spatial profiles or large-scale responses. A class is an observed label, rather than a second use of photometry already absorbed into a redshift distribution.

There are three physical sources of projected galaxies. Members occupy the distinguished halo. Galaxies in other nearby halos share its large-scale environment. More distant structures lie along the same sightline. We combine the latter two into an external population. External galaxies can be spatially close, strongly clustered, and numerous near the projected centre.

The simulation labels in this figure tell us which galaxies share a host. Those labels are available for a diagnostic; an observed catalogue has to infer the association. The distinction resembles the same-host and distinct-host separation of the halo model, but our question is local: the population associated with this particular halo, conditional on its region and selection.1

For class a, the latent intensity measure is

(2)Λa(dΩ,dz∣θ,F)=λaUa(ϑ∣θ)dΩδz∗(dz)+nR,a(z)Ha(ϑ,z∣θ)Fa(ϑ,z)dΩdz.

This is the architecture to justify, rather than an equation claimed to follow directly from gravity. The first term describes a compact angular population at an unresolved common distance. The second describes a selected reference population, its halo-conditioned mean modulation, and the realization of the surrounding structure.

Quantity Physical meaning
λa Expected selected member count inside the covered region
Ua Member profile per solid angle, with ∫DUadΩ=1
nR,a(z) Selected reference count per solid angle and redshift
Ha Mean enhancement or depletion conditional on the halo
Fa Positive residual environmental multiplier, with E[Fa∣θ]=1

The last condition is an ensemble statement. A particular region can contain more or fewer external galaxies than its average. We do not force its realization to integrate to the mean.

The inferred halo parameters are

(3)θ=(z∗,ϑ∗,{λa,rs,a,ϕa}a).

Classes share a centre and redshift; their scale radii rs,a and profile shapes ϕa may be tied or allowed to differ. A separately calibrated mass Mcal enters the environmental model. Identifying it with richness, or using it to fix a galaxy-profile radius, would require additional calibration.

We condition on D, its coverage mask, the galaxy selection, the reference population and the physical calibrations. Redshift integrals use a declared interval I⊂(0,∞) containing z∗. The model does not yet describe how the halo was discovered in a survey.

2. From a bound population to a projected profile

Geometry fixes the measure

Adopt a flat ΛCDM background with massless neutrinos and comoving distances. Writing the expansion rate as Hbg keeps it distinct from the environmental multiplier Ha. The distance and volume element are2

(4)χ(z)=clight∫0zdz′Hbg(z′),dVcom=χ2(z)clightHbg(z)dΩdz.

Thus a reference already measured per dΩdz corresponds to the effective comoving density

(5)n¯R,acom(z)=nR,a(z)Hbg(z)clightχ2(z).

This changes the measure; it does not predict the abundance a second time. In particular, multiplying a surface-redshift reference by another volume Jacobian would count that conversion twice.

Use a fixed equal-area local angular chart, so d2ϑ=dΩ. Its Euclidean separations approximate sky angles over the small region, giving

(6)R⊥≃χ(z∗)|ϑ−ϑ∗|.

Area preservation and distance accuracy are separate properties. The first controls counts; the second assigns a physical scale to a profile.

Projection explains the shape we observe

Gravity motivates a centrally concentrated tracer population. It does not specify a unique galaxy number-density law. Orbital structure, assembly and selection can produce different tracer profiles within comparable dark-matter halos.

Write a spherical mean tracer shape as n∗,acom(r)=n0,afϕa(r/rs,a). Integrating along a locally parallel line of sight gives its Abel projection:

(7)Σacom(R⊥)=n0,ars,aΣϕa(R⊥/rs,a),Σϕ(u)=2∫0∞fϕ(u2+t2)dt=2∫u∞sfϕ(s)s2−u2ds.

The projected distribution, rather than the three-dimensional profile itself, enters the observed angular intensity. Spherical symmetry describes a mean radial structure; it does not establish that this halo is spherical or relaxed.

Useful reference families are the NFW and Einasto forms,34

(8)fNFW(u)=1u(1+u)2,fEin(u)=exp(−2uαα),α>0.

These families describe collisionless halo structure. Applying them to selected galaxy counts is a tracer assumption: a fitted galaxy scale radius need not be the dark-matter scale radius.

Outer tapers and an unresolved projected core

A steeper outer envelope can be represented by

(9)ftNFW(u)=fNFW(u)(τ2u2+τ2)2,τ>1,ftEin(u)=fEin(u)[1+(u/τ)4]−3/2,τ>0.

The first is a smooth truncation family studied by Baltz, Marshall and Oguri.5 The second is a specified phenomenological taper. Neither expression derives a tidal boundary or a splashback surface.

For an NFW-based projection, a declared finite core may use

(10)Σϕ,core(u)=Σϕ(u2+ϵcore2),ϵcore>0.

This modifies the projected tracer law. It is neither the Abel projection of the original uncored shape nor automatically an average over uncertain centres. Einasto projections already have finite central values.

The aperture defines the richness

Absorb the surface-density amplitude and the factor χ2(z∗) into the expected selected count. Normalize the chosen projected law over the actual observed area:

(11)Ja(θ)=∫DΣϕa(χ(z∗)|ϑ−ϑ∗|rs,a)dΩ,Ua(ϑ∣θ)=1Ja(θ)Σϕa(χ(z∗)|ϑ−ϑ∗|rs,a).

Require 0<Ja<∞, and use the same chosen core or taper in both expressions. Moving the centre changes Ja, because the covered region captures a different fraction of the profile. A mask hole removes observed area; it does not imply a hole in the halo.

Consequently, λa refers to the selected, covered aperture. An untruncated NFW law can have a finite projected count in a bounded aperture despite a divergent whole-space integral. It supplies no whole-halo occupation without an extrapolation model.

The Dirac measure in the member term also has a domain of validity. A finite comoving depth L∥ and velocity dispersion σv imply approximate redshift scales

(12)Δzdepth∼Hbg(z∗)L∥clight,Δzvel∼(1+z∗)σvclight.

A thin halo is appropriate when its observational response varies little across these scales. Angular structure remains resolved while radial structure is unresolved. No orbital distribution or binding energy has been inferred.

3. A halo's surroundings differ from a random place

Growth and bias supply the large-scale excess

An overdensity attracts matter; expansion opposes its growth. Before shell crossing, the linearized pressureless continuity, Euler and Poisson equations yield6

(13)δ¨L+2Hbgδ˙L−4πGρ¯mδL=0,δL(k,z)=D+(z)δL(k,0),D+(0)=1.

No wavenumber appears in this growth equation. Scale-independent growth is appropriate to this linear pressureless regime; pressure, massive-neutrino free streaming and nonlinear mode coupling change the story.

For an isotropic field with the convention δL(r)=∫d3k(2π)−3δL(k)eik⋅r, the matter correlation is

(14)ξL(r,0)=∫0∞k2dk2π2PL(k,0)sin⁡krkr,ξL(r;z,z′)=D+(z)D+(z′)ξL(r,0).

The sine kernel comes from integrating a plane wave over directions. The power spectrum has units of comoving volume; ξL is dimensionless.

How the pressureless growth equation follows from dynamics

With scale factor asc=(1+z)−1, peculiar velocity v, and comoving gradients, the subhorizon Newtonian equations are

(15)δ˙m+1asc∇⋅[(1+δm)v]=0,v˙+Hbgv+1asc(v⋅∇)v=−1asc∇Φ,∇2Φ=4πGasc2ρ¯mδm.

Linearization removes products of perturbations. Differentiating the linear continuity equation and eliminating velocity divergence with Euler and Poisson gives the growth equation above. A single growing solution factorizes its time dependence into D+.

Halos respond to long-wavelength matter fluctuations through their abundance. Eulerian bias is defined by

(16)nh(M,z∣δℓ)=nh(M,z)[1+bh(M,z)δℓ+O(δℓ2)].

This response is distinct from the internal radial profile of one halo. We adopt a mass-only spherical-overdensity calibration, such as Tinker et al., with a consistent M200m convention.7 Its fitted coefficients are empirical inputs.

A galaxy population weights host abundances by occupation. If its selected occupation has no additional response to δℓ at fixed mass, its bias is

(17)ba(z)=∫dMnh(M,z)⟨Na∣M,z⟩bh(M,z)∫dMnh(M,z)⟨Na∣M,z⟩.

Rich hosts contribute more weight. Different selected populations can therefore have different biases. If occupation or photometric selection responds to environment at fixed mass and class, differentiating the occupation adds another term. Changing abundance alone does not justify reusing the same calibrated bias.

Conditioning on a halo has a precise meaning

A uniformly chosen location and a location occupied by a halo sample different environments. Conditioning on a point at an exact continuous location is formalized by a Palm distribution.8

Let ρh,a(2) be the mixed halo–galaxy pair density. Palm disintegration gives

(18)ρh,a(2)(r∗,r)=n¯hn¯acom[1+ξh,a(r∗,r)],ρa∣h!(r∣r∗)=ρh,a(2)(r∗,r)n¯h=n¯acom[1+ξh,a(r∗,r)].

The ratio is the probabilistic origin of a reference density multiplied by one plus a cross-correlation. It counts halo–galaxy pairs per expected conditioning halo.

The full pair density includes galaxies in the same host and in distinct hosts. Host identity must separate those contributions before a member profile is added to an external mean. The superscript ! removes the distinguished halo point from the halo process; it does not remove that halo's galaxies.

The identity behind halo-centred averaging

For the halo point process Nh and galaxy populations Ng, the reduced Campbell–Mecke identity is

(19)E[∑h∈Nhf(h,Nh∖{h},Ng)]=∫d3r∗ρh(r∗)Eh,r∗![f(r∗,Nh,Ng)].

Taking f to count galaxies in a small region makes the left side a pair count. Dividing its product density by the halo intensity gives the conditional galaxy intensity. Palm conditioning supplies this identity; it supplies neither a host assignment nor a small-scale exclusion prescription.

On large scales, δh≃bhδL and δa≃baδL, suggesting a distinct-host excess

(20)ξh,adist(d;z∗,z)≃bh(Mcal,z∗)ba(z)D+(z∗)D+(z)ξL(d,0).

The relevant separation is three-dimensional:

(21)dsph2=[χ(z)−χ(z∗)]2+2χ(z)χ(z∗)[1−cos⁡γ],d2≃[χ(z)−χ(z∗)]2+χ(z)χ(z∗)|ϑ−ϑ∗|2.

The local expression preserves line-of-sight separation. Angular overlap alone cannot produce a large correlation between galaxies at very different distances.

If baD+ varies slowly over distances with appreciable correlated weight, evaluate that amplitude near z∗. The adopted mean becomes

(22)Ha(ϑ,z∣θ)=1+Aa(z∗)E(d/R∗)ξL(d,0),Aa(z∗)=bh(Mcal,z∗)ba(z∗)D+2(z∗),R∗=[3Mcal4π200ρm,0]1/3.

Here Mcal=M200m. Multiplying the physical 200ρ¯m(z∗) radius by 1+z∗ cancels its redshift factors, producing this comoving transition scale. It does not fix rs,a.

Suppress the excess without deleting the reference population

Linear distinct-host bias does not describe bound galaxies in the halo interior. The transition E switches off the correlated excess near R∗. In the suppressed region, Ha=1. External galaxies can still contribute there.

For a fixed fractional half-width 0<wE<1, one definite smooth choice is

(23)E(s)={0,s≤1−wE,10t3−15t4+6t5,1−wE<s<1+wE,1,s≥1+wE,t=s−1+wE2wE.

The polynomial and width are phenomenological. This is not literal exclusion of every distinct-host galaxy. A strict exclusion law would require information about neighbouring hosts and a different conditional model.

The two profile measurements probe different geometries. Other halo centres can be depleted at small true separations, while external galaxies still populate projected annuli through their host extent and line-of-sight projection. A virial-radius cut is also not equivalent to a host label.

The measured curves do not calibrate the M200m transition directly: the export's adopted virial-radius convention differs from R∗. They demonstrate why a conditional mean is needed and why centre exclusion cannot simply be pasted into a projected galaxy model.

The correlation ξL can be negative, representing depletion. The requirement is positivity of the complete Ha throughout the modelled domain. An inadmissible full intensity cannot be repaired by silently flooring it. Where E=0, the excess is defined to vanish without evaluating a short-distance linear correlation.

4. The average environment is not this environment

A mean enhancement does not specify the group, filament or void along this particular sightline. Modelling only nR,aHa would assign the remaining count scatter to independent discreteness.

Instead, conditionally on a random intensity, let galaxies form a Poisson process. For a measurable region B,

(24)N(B)∣θ,F∼Poisson[Λ(B∣θ,F)].

Disjoint regions are independent conditional on the common field. Averaging over that field gives a Cox process.9 The random intensity is shared by many galaxies.

The law of total variance separates its two contributions:

(25)E[N(B)∣θ]=EF[Λ(B∣θ,F)],Var[N(B)∣θ]=EF[Λ(B∣θ,F)]+VarF[Λ(B∣θ,F)].

The first term is Poisson shot noise. The second describes variation of the underlying intensity. Matter-field covariance belongs to the second term; including catalogue shot noise in that covariance would count discreteness twice.

The conditional Poisson law is itself a closure. It leaves out residual central–satellite occupation structure and other correlations that may remain after a smooth intensity is specified. Members and external galaxies are assumed independent conditional on θ,F, so member occupation does not additionally respond to this particular environment at fixed halo parameters.

Why the mean does not determine the covariance

This separation is required by the hierarchy of point-process moments. A halo–galaxy pair correlation determines a conditional first moment. A conditional second moment also involves a halo and two distinct galaxies:

(26)ρh,a,b(3)n¯hn¯acomn¯bcom=1+ξh,a+ξh,b+ξa,b+ζh,a,b.

Palm disintegration and subtraction of conditional means then give

(27)ρa,b∣h!(2)−ρa∣h!ρb∣h!=n¯acomn¯bcom[ξa,b+ζh,a,b−ξh,aξh,b].

Factorial densities count distinct events, so the identical-galaxy shot-noise term is absent. Host separation requires corresponding host-restricted moments; it does not eliminate the need for higher-order information.

We therefore choose the residual field law separately. With KabF=Cov(Fa,Fb), the external intensity covariance is

(28)Cov(Λext,a,Λext,b)=nR,anR,bHaHbKabF,

where the spatial and redshift arguments are implicit. Specifying the fractional residual covariance independently of the inferred halo parameters is a declared conditional closure. It does not derive the missing halo-conditioned three-point function.

5. Which fluctuations survive projection?

Radial bands and angular cells set a physical resolution

A projected catalogue cannot recover every three-dimensional fluctuation. Declare angular cells and fixed radial bands Ir partitioning I. The multiplier Fa is assigned at that resolution; Ha can still vary within a cell or band.

This coarse graining describes a population field. An individual galaxy's uncertain redshift will be integrated through a separate observation channel.

The selected reference determines the radial weights:

(29)μar=∫IrnR,a(z)dz,war(z)=1Ir(z)nR,a(z)μar,∫wardz=1.

Only bands with μar>0 are used. A tentative biased tracer fluctuation is

(30)Δar(n^)=∫dzwar(z)ba(z)δm(χ(z)n^,z).

The weight follows by integrating nR,a(1+baδm) across the band and dividing by its reference abundance. In distance coordinates the same probability measure is φar(χ)dχ=war(z)dz, with φar(χ(z))=war(z)Hbg(z)/clight.

An overall rescaling of nR,a leaves this fractional covariance unchanged, while changing expected counts and shot noise. The weights use nR,a, rather than nR,aHa: this implements the choice to factor out the halo-dependent mean before prescribing the residual law.

A light cone requires correlations between different times

Define the unequal-time matter spectrum by

(31)⟨δm(k,z)δm(k′,z′)∗⟩=(2π)3δD(3)(k−k′)Pm(k;z,z′).

Fourier expansion gives the exact covariance of the tracer field just defined:

(32)⟨Δar(n^)Δas(n^′)⟩=∫dzdz′war(z)was(z′)ba(z)ba(z′)×∫d3k(2π)3Pm(k;z,z′)eik⋅[χ(z)n^−χ(z′)n^′].

It is exact for this biased field, with its stated omissions, rather than an exact observed-galaxy covariance. Peculiar velocities and other projection effects have not entered.

An equal-time nonlinear spectrum specifies amplitudes at each epoch, but does not specify their temporal coherence. Write10

(33)Pm(k;z,z′)=rm(k;z,z′)PNL(k,z)PNL(k,z′),|rm|≤1.

Setting rm=1 follows from coherent linear growth when the spectra are linear. With nonlinear spectra it is an extra approximation.

Using PL for the large-scale mean and PNL for residual covariance serves different purposes. The latter can describe clustering inside unresolved external structures. Extending a scale-independent galaxy bias into those nonlinear scales is an effective assumption; the combination is not a systematic expansion of a single joint theory.

Retaining radial phases gives a coherent local construction

Resolve a mode into radial wavenumber k∥ and angular transverse wavenumber ℓ. At distance χ, its physical transverse wavenumber is ℓ/χ. The Jacobian d2k⊥=d2ℓ/χ2 contributes 1/χ to an amplitude.

Under a coherent local driving approximation, define

(34)har(k∥,ℓ)=∫dzwar(z)ba(z)χ(z)PNL(k∥2+ℓ2/χ2(z),z)×eik∥χ(z).

The factors identify the selected population, its response to matter, the fluctuation amplitude, the angular conversion and the radial phase. The response has units Mpc1/2. Its angular spectral covariance is dimensionless:

(35)Ba,rs(ℓ)=∫−∞∞dk∥2πhar(k∥,ℓ)has(k∥,ℓ)∗=∫0∞dk∥πRe[har(k∥,ℓ)has(k∥,ℓ)∗].

For any real band coefficients vr,

(36)∑r,svrBa,rs(ℓ)vs=∫−∞∞dk∥2π|∑rvrhar(k∥,ℓ)|2≥0.

Shared amplitudes make this a positive semidefinite covariance. Individual cross-correlations need not all be positive.

There is a second approximation here. The same angular mode is coherently driven at different distances even though ℓ/χ(z) changes its three-dimensional transverse wavenumber. The unequal-time geometric mean for the same physical wavenumber does not justify that identification by itself. The construction approaches an ordinary Cartesian projection over a narrow distance range; over a broad range it remains a specified local light-cone closure.

Because it retains radial phases, it is not a Limber approximation. Broad radial weights cancel rapidly oscillating modes. Nearby or overlapping bands can retain shared fluctuations.

The angular window is part of the model

Let W be a normalized cell-averaging window. Averaging both entries of a covariance supplies the squared Fourier window:

(37)Ka,rs(Δ)=∫d2ℓ(2π)2|W^(ℓ)|2Ba,rs(ℓ)cos⁡(ℓ⋅Δ).

For a rectangular cell,

(38)W^(ℓ)=sinc(ℓxδx/2)sinc(ℓyδy/2),sinc(u)=sin⁡uu.

The window removes sensitivity to structure far below the cell scale. Finite variance requires the integral to converge; an arbitrarily fine limit is not assumed.

A partially covered cell still describes the physical fluctuation over that cell. Only its covered area contributes observed counts. The mask restricts observation, rather than forcing the underlying field to vanish. Also, a fixed angular width represents a physical transverse width proportional to χ(z), rather than a uniform three-dimensional voxel.

6. A positive law for the unresolved environment

Compression motivates a multiplicative description

A Gaussian additive prescription F=1+Δ permits negative intensities. A positive field must allow large overdensities while respecting the lower bound at zero.

The nonlinear continuity equation offers a motivation. Along a single-stream trajectory,

(39)DDtln⁡(1+δm)=−1asc∇⋅v,DDt=∂∂t+vasc⋅∇.

Compression accumulates additively in log density and multiplicatively in density. Approximating accumulated compression by a Gaussian motivates a lognormal law.11 Shell crossing, trajectory weighting and nonlinear velocity statistics prevent this from being a proof about the Eulerian matter field.

We impose the law directly on the coarse-grained intensity multipliers. With indices i=(a,j,r) for class, angular cell and radial band,

(40)g∼N(0,C),Fi=exp(gi−12Cii).

The Gaussian field describes the residual log intensity. Conditional Poisson sampling makes the latent external population a log-Gaussian Cox process.12

The Gaussian exponential identity E[etTg]=etTCt/2 immediately gives

(41)E[Fi]=1,E[FiFj]=eCij,Cov(Fi,Fj)=eCij−1.

The half-variance correction preserves the ensemble mean. It does not force every finite realization to have the same total.

The count distribution becomes broader even though its ensemble mean is unchanged. Neighbouring cells can rise or fall together because they share modes. At zero field variance, the intensity reduces to its mean and only Poisson discreteness remains.

Covariance matching has an existence condition

Matching the projected target covariance requires the entrywise transform

(42)Ca,rs(Δ)=ln⁡[1+Ka,rs(Δ)].

Require finite variances, 1+Kij>0, and positive semidefiniteness of the resulting C on the modelled indices. A positive semidefinite K alone does not guarantee a positive semidefinite ln⁡(1+K). If the transform fails, the chosen lognormal closure cannot represent that target covariance.

The order matters. We first average the tracer fluctuation at a declared resolution, then impose a lognormal law at that scale. Averaging a finer lognormal field does not generally produce another exact lognormal field. Changing the resolution calls for reconsidering the closure.

The assumed Gaussian law also fixes every higher intensity moment:

(43)E[∏q=1mFiq]=exp[∑q<tCiqit].

Agreement with a two-point spectrum therefore does not establish agreement with the halo-conditioned higher-order moments. These are predictions of the closure.

Different populations can share modes, with an explicit dependence assumption

Let Sa(ℓ) be the admissible spectral covariance of the class-a Gaussian log field across radial bands, on one fixed common homogeneous angular domain. A definite common-mode prescription is

(44)Sab(ℓ)=Sa(ℓ)1/2Sb(ℓ)1/2,Sba=Sab†.

Use Hermitian principal square roots. The auto-covariances are retained, and joint positivity follows from

(45)∑a,bva†Sabvb=‖∑aSa1/2va‖2≥0.

This assumes shared log-field driving without an additional independent class-specific component. In the one-band case, nonzero log-field modes have unit cross-class coherence. Counts can remain imperfectly correlated because intensities, projection and Poisson sampling differ.

The prescription does not follow from the galaxy bias formula. It need not equal a cross-class covariance obtained by projecting distinct matter responses and jointly transforming them. It is an explicit dependence closure.

An exact Palm example clarifies the scope of the conditional construction

Suppose, for comparison, that halo and galaxy intensities were jointly log-Gaussian and conditionally independent Poisson populations. A halo occurrence weights field realizations by their halo intensity:13

(46)Eh![Ψ]=E[Λh(r∗)Ψ]E[Λh(r∗)].

If gh and gg are centred halo and galaxy log intensities, Gaussian exponential moments give

(47)Eh![etTgg]=exp[tTCgh+12tTCggt].

The galaxy log-field mean shifts by Cgh, while its covariance remains Cgg. Its intensity mean is multiplied by

(48)HajointLG(r∣r∗)=exp⁡[Ca,h(r,r∗)].

This exact example explains how a modulated mean and an unchanged residual log covariance can coexist under conditioning. It does not prove that our bias-based Ha and nonlinear residual covariance are the Palm law of a single global process. That stronger claim would require log⁡Ha to be an admissible cross-covariance in a joint Gaussian model. Positivity of Ha alone is insufficient.

7. From true distance to a galaxy's redshift information

A redshift PDF needs an observation law

The latent process lives at true redshift. The catalogue contains photometric information represented by a normalized density pd(z).

Normalization over z does not make that density a likelihood for the datum at fixed z. If a measurement likelihood and source prior produced a posterior, Bayes' rule reads

(49)p(z∣d)=ℓ(d∣z)π0(z)∫ℓ(d∣z′)π0(z′)dz′.

Using the posterior as a likelihood retains its prior weighting. The original likelihood may be unrecoverable when the source prior, support or marginalized nuisance variables are unknown.

Here we choose a different, explicit route: a normalized empirical observation channel defined by the supplied redshift distributions and their selected reference population. This is a declared empirical model, whose physical use still requires calibration.

Read the empirical joint distribution in the required direction

A fixed parent population of area Ωref defines a data-template measure

(50)νa(dd)=1Ωref∑j:aj=aδdj(dd).

It has units of templates per solid angle. Let R(d)∈{0,1} define selection. For example, admit a template if its probability in a fixed redshift window exceeds a fixed threshold.

Define the joint reference, its redshift marginal, and its conditional channel:

(51)Ja(dz,dd)=R(d)pd(z)dzνa(dd),nR,a(z)=∫R(d)pd(z)νa(dd),κa(d∣z)=R(d)pd(z)nR,a(z),nR,a(z)>0.

At fixed redshift, the channel is normalized over possible observed templates:

(52)∫κa(d∣z)νa(dd)=1,Ja=nR,a(z)dzκa(d∣z)νa(dd).

The same joint measure can be read as a redshift distribution for each template or as a distribution over templates at each redshift. The latter is the direction needed to observe the latent point process.

Over full reference support,

(53)∫nR,a(z)dz=∫R(d)νa(dd)=NR,aΩref.

Abundance and the relative occurrence of templates come from one reference. The denominator in κa is not an assertion about the prior originally used to generate each PDF.

The normalization identities are exact for this empirical construction. Interpreting its latent coordinate as true redshift requires calibrated PDFs. Transferring the same channel to member and external populations additionally assumes that redshift and class capture the relevant differences in photometric properties. A population label does not guarantee that assumption.

Local channel averaging does not resolve halo dynamics

For members, a declared local probability kernel Qz∗ can average the channel:

(54)κa∗(d∣z∗)=∫Iκa(d∣z′)Qz∗(dz′),Qz∗(I)=1,∫κa∗(d∣z∗)νa(dd)=1.

The kernel is fixed, local, normalized and shared across classes and templates. The unsmoothed case is Qz∗=δz∗. This averages observational responses while the latent member population remains thin at z∗; it does not infer a velocity distribution or alter the external channel.

Reference support must be positive wherever a channel is used. If I covers only part of a template's PDF, restrict the integrals without separately renormalizing every galaxy's retained tail. Channel normalization is over templates at fixed redshift, rather than over the admitted redshift interval for each galaxy.

8. The observed process keeps positions and counts

Two latent populations become two competing event intensities

Mark each latent galaxy using its normalized channel, then discard its true redshift and host label. Independent marking and mapping preserve conditional Poisson sampling; superposed component intensities add.9

Relative to dΩνa(dd), the observed intensity is qa=Pa+Ea, where

(55)Pa(ϑ,d∣θ)=λaUa(ϑ∣θ)κa∗(d∣z∗),Ea(ϑ,d∣θ,F)=∫InR,a(z)HaFaκa(d∣z)dz=R(d)∫Ipd(z)HaFadz.

Membership tests compatibility with one common halo redshift. The external explanation integrates along every admitted distance.

The cancellation of nR,a in the external event term follows from the empirical channel. It does not remove abundance from the model. Abundance remains in the template measure and in the expected count. Since κa has solid-angle units and Ua inverse-solid-angle units, the two event intensities can be added consistently.

This explorer uses the unsmoothed empirical channel. A galaxy's PDF is held fixed while the candidate redshift and competing environmental enhancement change. A secondary mode can increase the external contribution even when the largest PDF peak lies near the candidate.

The displayed allocation is conditional on the chosen state. It is not a fitted membership probability. A posterior result would average over common halo parameters and possible environments.

Expected galaxies that were not observed carry information

Integrating qa over the covered sky and all possible templates gives

(56)A(θ,F)=∑aλa+Aext(θ,F),Aext=∑a∫DdΩ∫IdznR,a(z)Ha(ϑ,z)Fa(ϑ,z).

The normalized profile and channels make the member contribution exactly its selected-covered expected count.

Conditional Poisson probabilities give the point-pattern likelihood

(57)L(X∣θ,F)∝e−A(θ,F)∏i(Pi+Ei),log⁡L=∑ilog⁡(Pi+Ei)−∑aλa−Aext.

The exponential term includes empty regions of observation space: extra predicted galaxies were not observed. Dropping it would reward arbitrarily large intensities. Conditioning on the observed count would instead ask a different question and discard abundance information.

For each galaxy, the order is consequential: integrate over its uncertain redshift, add the competing origins, then take one logarithm. An expression such as ∫pi(z)log⁡Λ(z)dz performs a different operation. Nor can a PDF be treated as a collection of independent fractional galaxies.

After marginalizing F, the observed process remains Cox, but generally ceases to be log-Gaussian. Integrating lognormal intensities and adding a member intensity does not preserve a Gaussian logarithm.

Shared environments must be marginalized together

With a proper halo prior πθ and the Gaussian field law ΠG,

(58)Π(dθ,dg∣X)∝L(X∣θ,F(g))πθ(dθ)ΠG(dg).

The posterior requires positive finite evidence, locally finite intensities, finite profile normalizers and suitable prior behaviour near singular profile limits. Halo parameters and the field are assumed prior independent conditional on the fixed calibrations.

The environment-marginal likelihood is

(59)Lmarg(X∣θ)∝EF[e−A(θ,F)∏i(Pi+Ei(F))].

Replacing F by one, inserting a best-fit map, or separately averaging each event contribution does not perform this marginalization. Several galaxies may share one alternative structure, so their explanations are coupled.

A halo prior based on independent information can enter in the ordinary way. If the candidate, aperture or prior was chosen using the same photometry, this remains a conditional empirical refinement. A survey-wide discovery-and-selection posterior would require an additional generative model.

9. What membership and richness uncertainty mean

Membership compares explanations of the same observation

Let Zi=1 indicate the primary population. Conditional on the common parameters and field, superposition gives

(60)wi(θ,F)=Pr(Zi=1∣X,θ,F)=PiPi+Ei.

Angular concentration, redshift support, class and external structure all enter. A neighbouring group can increase Ei even close to the projected centre. A compact collection compatible with one common redshift can increase support for the primary explanation.

The posterior membership is

(61)w¯i=Pr(Zi=1∣X)=∫wi(θ,F(g))Π(dθ,dg∣X).

This is an average of conditional ratios, rather than a ratio of averaged intensities. It is statistical host association under the assumed model, not a calculation of a galaxy's orbital binding energy.

Likewise, ∑iw¯i estimates the realized member count among the observations. The parameter λa is an underlying expected selected count. Their interpretations differ.

For an external galaxy, retaining its latent redshift gives

(62)Pr(zi∈dz∣Zi=0,X,θ,F)=pdi(z)Hai(ϑi,z)Fai(ϑi,z)∫Ipdi(t)Hai(ϑi,t)Fai(ϑi,t)dtdz.

Structure reweights the PDF support at each distance. It can resolve a mode or preserve several competing modes. If the observation channel has no redshift dependence, it supplies no individual photometric discrimination; the remaining information comes from other observables or assumptions.

Shared structure couples uncertainty

In a fixed sky region B, let MB denote the integrated member plus external intensity. At fixed θ,

(63)Var(NB∣θ)=E[NB∣θ]+∑a,b∫B×IdΩdz∫B×IdΩ′dz′nR,anR,bHaHbKabF.

The second term is nonnegative as a whole even if some separated regions anticorrelate. These are ensemble count moments, rather than an uncertainty assigned retrospectively to an already observed fixed count.

Membership labels are independent conditional on θ,F, but generally dependent after these shared quantities are marginalized. For the realized member count S=∑iZi,

(64)Var(S∣X)=∑iw¯i(1−w¯i)+2∑i<jCov(Zi,Zj∣X).

For distinct galaxies, the covariance equals the posterior covariance of their conditional probabilities wi,wj. Its sign is not fixed. Summing independent Bernoulli variances drops the coupling and is not generally conservative.

The useful limits make the assumptions visible

Choice Physical question retained
Ha=1, random Fa A clustered external universe without the distinguished halo's mean excess
Halo-dependent Ha, Fa≡1 The average halo environment, with only conditional Poisson discreteness
Ha=Fa=1 The ordinary selected reference population

Removing field variance is different from setting g=0 at nonzero variance: the latter gives Fi=e−Cii/2, not one.

The strongest approximations occur where physical regimes are joined: a spherical galaxy tracer profile, large-scale bias with an excess-only transition, nonlinear matter power with coherent local light-cone driving, a finite-scale lognormal law, common log-field modes across classes, and a transferable empirical observation channel.

A reliable application must test those choices together under the same selection. Useful checks include projected host-separated profiles, field covariance after accounting for shot noise and overlapping apertures, calibrated redshift responses, posterior predictive angular counts, membership reliability against mock host labels, and coverage for halo parameters in controlled generative simulations.

The catalogue figures here establish none of those posterior-performance claims. They expose the physical ingredients that need modelling. Triaxial member structure, resolved velocities, assembly-dependent or scale-dependent bias, magnification and uncertain fixed calibrations remain outside this construction.

Richness consequently comes from the entire chain: halo structure, conditional clustering, possible environmental realizations, the observation channel and the count-preserving likelihood. A coherent alternative along the sightline is part of the inference.

Data and reproducibility

The empirical figures are regenerated from the supplied Flagship Parquet export.14 It contains 34,459,985 raw rows in one nested order-3 HEALPix pixel, covering {{area_deg2}} square degrees. The export selection was positive H-band flux and HAB<26; the figures consistently apply the brighter HAB<24 cut, retaining 9,950,200 galaxies.

For these diagnostics, use h=0.67, Ωm=0.319, and a flat matter-plus-Λ distance calculation. The photometric selection follows the export query's cgs flux convention, HAB=−2.5log10⁡fν−48.6. Masses adopt lmhalo=log10⁡[M/(M⊙/h)], so the physical 1014M⊙ threshold is lmhalo≥log10⁡(0.67×1014).

The export lacks an explicit radius-unit header. We adopt comoving h−1 kpc for its virial radius and retain an internal Bryan–Norman mass–radius consistency check in the provenance. This check supports the convention; it does not authenticate missing metadata or equate that radius with the theoretical M200m transition.

What the catalogue measurements contain

The projected profiles use 702 interior halos with M≥1014M⊙ and 0.4≤zh<1. The default narrower sample has 360 halos with 1014≤M/M⊙<3×1014 and 0.5≤zh<0.8.

For each halo, logarithmic annuli span 0.1–5rvir. The redshift-space cylinder has half-depth 20h−1 comoving Mpc around the central galaxy's observed redshift. For any counted population,

(65)Σh,j=Nh,jπrvir,h2(xj+12−xj2),Σ―j=1Nh∑hΣh,j.

Total, member-host and external counts use identical selections, so their decomposition is exact. The central at R=0 lies below the first bin. Curves are equal-halo means. Twelve matched random sightlines per halo share the radius, redshift and geometric boundary requirement.

Every aperture has a densely sampled great-circle boundary at 5.05rvir inside the export footprint. We assume that geometric footprint is complete at the adopted magnitude cut; no additional survey completeness mask was supplied.

The centre diagnostic uses other selected centrals at their hosts' true redshifts, spherical shell volumes and a reference density in zh±0.025. It does not reconstruct missing real-space satellite coordinates. Bands in both views show the 16th–84th percentile spread across halos. Mass/redshift mixing, discreteness and overlapping neighbourhoods prevent interpreting that spread as an inferred field covariance or an error on the mean.

What the mathematical illustrations contain

The scene uses a fixed 12-by-12-arcminute patch and a previously chosen aligned halo pair. The full cut contains 7,341 rows; the projection figure follows all 183 primary-host and 96 aligned-host galaxies. The pair was chosen to illustrate overlap.

Galaxy numbers in this export are local to each host. Figure labels use the pair of halo ID and galaxy number to identify an observation uniquely.

No photometric-redshift PDFs were supplied. The PDFs used in the projection and response figures are explicit synthetic mixtures in s=ln⁡(1+z), with weights 0.04,0.92,0.04, alias shifts −0.25,0,0.25, and a magnitude-dependent main width 0.015+0.035clip[(H−20)/4,0,1]. They are normalized on 0<z<3.2 and never renormalized when the displayed redshift range changes.

The response explorer's reference is the mean PDF of 4,096 deterministically selected mock templates, including the three illustrated data templates so that they belong to the empirical observation measure's support. Its primary response is 0.15pi(z∗)/πR(z∗); its external response is ∫pi(z)[1+Aexp⁡(−(z−zneighbour)2/(2×0.0182))]dz. This is a teaching instance of the empirical channel, rather than source-prior removal or a survey-calibrated reference.

The field figure is a separate mathematical illustration. It uses a specified finite set of Gaussian Fourier modes, a smooth positive mean and conditional Poisson samples. The covariance and half-variance correction are exact for that finite construction. Its modes are not presented as a fit to Flagship or an evaluation of PNL.

The printable SVGs and compact figure data are linked below. The interactive views use the same generated measurements and remain optional; the text, mathematics and printable figures are available without JavaScript.
